amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule, whether a nominal anchor or a prepositional predicate.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַּת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַּת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: DEU.18 wrote the tripartite nominal clause twice and analysed it two ways: 18.2 gave the single 'is' of יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ to the resuming pronoun, while 18.22 gave 'that' to הוּא and the copula to the predicate דָּבָר, matching 18.3 and 18.12. Rule 20 as written settles the second shape but is silent on the first, where the pronoun has no English of its own and the copula is the only word standing in its slot — which is exactly what led the verse pass to reach for the present-morpheme reasoning of rules 46-48. The added sentences close that gap in place rather than leaving the over-broad silence for the next reader, and they cite rule 22 for the unrendered resumption and rule 51 for the pronoun that already holds a word. This is a qualification of rule 20's own copula sentence, so it is an amendment and not a new rule.

conventions: Where the ASV renders a finite Hebrew verb adverbially and a complement infinitive carries the English predicate, the adverb belongs to the finite verb and the English verb to the infinitive: יָזִיד ... לְדַבֵּר דָּבָר -> 'shall speak a word presumptuously' (18.20) gives 'presumptuously' to יָזִיד and 'shall speak' to the infinitive, and לֹא אֹסֵף לִשְׁמֹעַ -> 'Let me not hear again' (18.16) gives 'Let me ... again' to אֹסֵף and 'hear' to the infinitive. Where no second verb morpheme stands, the English predicate the ASV supplies to complete that adverbial rendering stays inside the finite verb's own unit rather than being marked added: הֵיטִיבוּ אֲשֶׁר דִּבֵּרוּ -> 'They have well said that which they have spoken' (18.17) keeps 'said' with הֵיטִיבוּ, headed on 'well' under rule 44.

In the divination list of 18.10-11 the ASV writes one English agent noun for a whole Hebrew phrase. חֹבֵר חָבֶר -> 'a charmer' and דֹרֵשׁ אֶל־הַמֵּתִים -> 'a necromancer' are read as rule 30 fusions headed on the participle, with the supplied indefinite article joining the nominal expression under rule 15. The article of הַמֵּתִים stands outside the fused unit as unrepresented, since the English word carries no article's sense — the division rule 30 already makes for דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים -> 'chronicles'.

report: One genuine cross-verse split: placement of the verbless-clause copula. DEU.18.22 (הוּא הַדָּבָר -> 'that is the thing') puts the copula on the predicate דָּבָר and gives הוּא only its own 'that', matching DEU.18.3 ('whether it be ox') and DEU.18.12 ('is an abomination'). DEU.18.2 (יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ -> 'Jehovah is their inheritance') instead gave the 'is' to הוּא and left the predicate bare. Rule 20 sends the copula to the predicate and gives an explicit subject only its own English; the ASV realizes this subject once, as 'Jehovah', so the resuming הוּא is the unrendered occurrence under rule 22. DEU.18.2 is patched to the shape 18.22 already has, discontinuous around the suffix's 'their' as 18.22 is discontinuous around the article's 'the'.

Checked and licensed, not split: the preposition-plus-construct pairs are uniform on rule 30's one-rendering condition. One English word fuses (בְּקֶרֶב -> among, לִפְנֵי -> before, מֵאֵת -> from, מֵעִם -> of, לְבַד -> besides, בִגְלַל -> because of, בְּזָדוֹן -> presumptuously); two English words split (מִקֶּרֶב -> from among in 18.18, מִפְּנֵי -> from before in 18.12). Every fused unit heads as rules 23 and 24 direct.

וְלֹא is split where the ASV writes two words and fused where it writes one, both ways within one verse twice over (18.16 'that ... not' beside 'neither'; 18.22 'if ... not' beside 'nor'). That is rule 35 read off the English, not an inconsistency.

Rule 41's determiner count is uniform across 18.9, 18.12, 18.14, 18.16 and 18.20: the demonstrative takes the phrase's one written determiner, every article goes unrepresented, and a governing construct takes a supplied 'the'. Rule 29's two branches are both used correctly — 18.3 'the priests due' is the possessive recasting, so the written 'the' goes to the article on כֹּהֲנִים; 18.16 'the day of the assembly' is the arthrous case, so each morpheme takes the 'the' before its own word.

The four `added` units each survive their rule: the italic 'even' (18.1) and 'as for' (18.14) under rule 16's limits on the appositional and fronting families, 'to do' (18.14) under rule 34's supplied-lexical-verb boundary, 'it' (18.19) under rule 44's supplied-object sentence. None is folded into a neighbouring rendering to avoid the label.

Examined and deliberately left alone: the chapter labels rule-30 fusions `aligned` in fifteen places and `noncompositional` in two (כָּל־הַיָּמִים -> 'for ever', דֹרֵשׁ אֶל־הַמֵּתִים -> 'a necromancer'), while הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר -> 'whosoever' is `aligned`. The corpus carries both labels for the identical construction (לִפְנֵי -> before is 364 aligned and 263 noncompositional; כָּל הַ -> whosoever is both), and the 'for ever' unit matches its own precedent exactly. Edges and heads are unaffected, so there is nothing to correct and nothing promotable.

BSB: no genuine error. Every disagreement is a documented convention difference — paragogic nun (rule 32 names BSB as the disagreeing party), prepositions silenced by recasting (rule 40), articles under rules 29/41/47, the repeated חֵלֶק of 18.8 and the resumptive suffix of 18.22 under rule 22, and the bare apodosis waw of 18.20 under rule 14. No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.
Which חֵלֶק of 18.8 carries the single 'portions' remains a genuine tie; the verse note records the choice and the alternative, and I did not disturb it.
